messages.subject: Re: mirtCAT reverse-code likert scale
messages.subject_clean: mirtCAT reverse-code likert scale
messages.body_plain:
Good question. In mirtCAT I assume that the data will be collected in a form that would have been passed directly to mirt(). So in your case, what you would see in the IRT estimates is that the slope parameter (the a's) will be in the negative direction without reversing the score ordering. To account for this in your CAT application then, just initialise the item parameters that are collected with a reverse scoring format with the negative of the slope parameter instead. So if your GRM had the parameters [a1=1.2, d1=4, d2=0, d3=-1], then just use [a1= -1*1.2, d1=4, d2=0, d3=-1] instead. HTH.

Phil

Interesting question. It looks like lattice doesn't track colour/theme changes very well (this is where I sometimes wish the plots in mirt were written with ggplot2). In your plot you need to modify the output type as well in the legend, which is generated by the auto.key input. Here's an example:

library(mirt)
mod <- mirt(Science, 1)
trellis.device(color=FALSE)
itemplot(mod, 1, type = 'trace', auto.key=list(points=FALSE, lines=TRUE))

I suppose in mirt the legend should be using lines by default anyway rather than points, so perhaps I'll change this internally to ensure everything is kosher where it should be. Cheers.

Phil

2) what if there is some missing for the 13 items, e.g. just having 12 items' responses?

Thanks for any comments/helps in advance!

Yingyi

2) what about identification of this model in 'mirt'?

3) can i use  'impute' option (as the only option) in M2 for fitting of the model to data?

Best

cfa_pc <- cfa(mod_cfa_pc, data=ds_bdi_pc, estimator = 'WLSMV', ordered=names(base_bdi_pc))
fitMeasures(cfa_pc, c("aic","chisq", "df", "pvalue", "cfi", "rmsea"))
aic  chisq     df pvalue    cfi  rmsea
NA 27.794 14.000  0.015  0.999  0.038

Thus, I ran the graded model.
graded_pc <- mirt(ds_bdi_pc, 1, itemtype = "graded", method = "MHRM") #create the model
M2(graded_pc)
Error: M2() statistic cannot be calculated due to too few degrees of freedom

M2(graded_pc, type="C2")
M2 df p RMSEA RMSEA_5 RMSEA_95      SRMSR       TLI CFI
stats -15.2803 14 1     0       0        0 0.03171308 -1.838626   0

Do you have any suggestion ?

> Hello again Phil,

>
> e.g., mod_configural <- multipleGroup(items, Q2, group = group1,
>                                 invariance=c('free_means', 'free_var'))

This likely is not identified. Configural invariance is essentially completely independent (and independently identified) single group models; hence, if you took a subset of the data within each group and fit a model to that then the sum of the log-likelihood values would equal this config. Freeing the hyper mean/var parameters would only be possible if there are anchor items selected.

>
> METRIC/WEAK: "invariance=c('slopes'))"
>
> e.g., mod_metric <- multipleGroup(items, Q2, group = group1, invariance=c('slopes'))
>
> STRONG/SCALAR:  invariance=c('slopes', 'intercepts', 'free_means'))

>                             invariance=c('slopes', 'intercepts', 'free_means'))

>

>
> e.g., mod_strict <- multipleGroup(items, Q2, group = group1,
>                             invariance=c('slopes', 'intercepts'))
>
> This is a naive/obvious question, but are the options listed above just broad strokes for the same function that CONSTRAINB does on individual items/parameters?

Correct. I can't really confirm whether these are exact (the strict looks correct...groups are completely equal, even in terms of their latent trait distributions). IRT models don't perfectly fit this convention because there's really no such thing as a residual variance term (these parameters are not uniquely identified in IRT models compared to SEM, so that part falls out).

>
> Lastly, after multigroup, do I need to run the DIF analyses separately for polytomous and dichotomous items, since they have a different number of d parameters?

Depends on your approach, such as via likelihood ratio tests, Wald tests, or even (finally) my DRF statistics:  https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11336-018-9626-9
But typically you isolate items one at a time and go from there, so via the automated DIF() function this could be a little more difficult (may require you to make two separate sweep runs, one for all dichotomous items then another for all related polytomous items). HTH.

Not really, they have to be selected based on prior theory. Yes, that's fine and indeed appropriate. Anchor items should contribute 0 to the effect size magnitude in DBF bundles because the response curves across groups are identical.

>
> Question 2. Does  empirical_ES use the original anchor items from the model_anchor1.3?

Yes.

> 1 1850351 1850394 1854351 1856840 -924392.7    NaN NaN   NaN

>
> $rmc02
>       AIC    AICc   SABIC     BIC    logLik     X2  df     p
> 1 1850342 1850385 1854342 1856831 -924388.0    NaN NaN   NaN
> 2 1850340 1850383 1854365 1856870 -924381.9 12.291   5 0.031
>
> etc.
>
> Is there a way to get these stats at the bundle level? I tried anova (x,y) but I guess anova doesn't work with DIF. Perhaps I could run MultipleGroup model with CONSTRAINB to model DBF but I am not sure what that would look like. Although perhaps the empirical_ES is sufficient in terms of reporting? Sorry, getting a bit turned around here. Thank you in advance for any advice you could offer!

This approach identifies items with DIF, and are basically more flexible models than the constrained one. If you want to be testing for DBF you have to allow for the effects of DIF for each suspicious item in the same fitted model, and after that has been fitted test whether the aggregate effects of the DIF items results in an overall bundle bias effect. So, given this information, you would need to fit a new, more flexible model first, and then use the DRF()/empirical_ES() functions to test for DBF. HTH.

> Phil

> I did use QMC=T for M2. So, for model selection I would trust more the likelihoods.
>
> Given the "curse of dimensionality", the M2 fit indices are not as reliable then?

I think at some point and for some models the M2 statistic could break. Like all statistics it's possible for it to fail for numerical reasons as well, so it's possible there's just something extreme about your observations causing problems too (e.g., intercepts could be too large, slopes are tending to infinity, etc). It's likely too hard to tell without looking rather close to a reproducible example.

>
> I ask because I am used to evaluate fit from the SEM perspective, and coming from that having a better likelihood but worst RMSEA doesnt make sense. Clearly I dont know the difference of those in IRT.

RMSEA is a function of the degrees of freedom and general goodness of fit as a chi-square variate, so more complicated models often can and do have larger RMSEA values if the decrease in df and model fit are not traded off well (that's largely the point of these fit stats, and is true in SEM as well). This is also true of the other measures CFI, TLI, etc. The log-likelihood test just states that one model is more likely than the other in terms of predicting the data, not that it is an effective representation of the data or that the (potentially large) decrease in df (and therefore increase in model complexity).

That all said, the log-likelihood and M2 statistics really are focusing on different data aspects. M2 is focusing on uni/bivariate moments only, and collapsing the high-dimensional tables of counts to these moments, while the log-likelihood is computed row-wise in the data itself and therefore contains all moments without collapsing.

>
> A side question about MHRM, is this bayesian estimation or is it using the metropolis hastings for integration in the maximum likelihood? As this is the type of sampler that Stan uses for general bayesian.

Just as an integration for the random effect components. It only becomes a Bayesian estimator if you include prior parameter distributions explicitly. HTH.

> I think at some point and for some models the M2 statistic could break. Like all statistics it's possible for it to fail for numerical reasons as well, so it's possible there's just something extreme about your observations causing problems too (e.g., intercepts could be too large, slopes are tending to infinity, etc). It's likely too hard to tell without looking rather close to a reproducible example.
>
> >
> > I ask because I am used to evaluate fit from the SEM perspective, and coming from that having a better likelihood but worst RMSEA doesnt make sense. Clearly I dont know the difference of those in IRT.
>
> RMSEA is a function of the degrees of freedom and general goodness of fit as a chi-square variate, so more complicated models often can and do have larger RMSEA values if the decrease in df and model fit are not traded off well (that's largely the point of these fit stats, and is true in SEM as well). This is also true of the other measures CFI, TLI, etc. The log-likelihood test just states that one model is more likely than the other in terms of predicting the data, not that it is an effective representation of the data or that the (potentially large) decrease in df (and therefore increase in model complexity).
>
> That all said, the log-likelihood and M2 statistics really are focusing on different data aspects. M2 is focusing on uni/bivariate moments only, and collapsing the high-dimensional tables of counts to these moments, while the log-likelihood is computed row-wise in the data itself and therefore contains all moments without collapsing.
>
> >
> > A side question about MHRM, is this bayesian estimation or is it using the metropolis hastings for integration in the maximum likelihood? As this is the type of sampler that Stan uses for general bayesian.

> Just as an integration for the random effect components. It only becomes a Bayesian estimator if you include prior parameter distributions explicitly. HTH.

The former test when using the MH-RM algorithm computes the log-likelihood via stochastic integration, so should be relatively free of the "curse-of-dimensionality" problem, whereas M2 computes the values using standard numerical integration (which gets less accurate as the number of traits increases). messages.body_plain:
Hi Danilo,

What is an oblique bifactor model? By definition, bifactor models are orthogonal in their latent traits. Otherwise, the model may not be properly identified. It is however possible to obtain exploratory bifactor models post-rotation by a) fitting an exploratory model with K factors extracted and b) using summary(mod, rotate = 'bifactorT')  (or 'bifactorQ').

Phil
